meaning: after 得 / 不: can / cannot manage (吃不了 can't finish; 受不了 can't stand)

senses.en: V + 不了 / V + 得了: cannot / can (manage to do it, get through all of it)
in fixed phrases: 受不了 can't stand it; 忘不了 can't forget; 少不了 can't do without

examples.zh: 菜太多了，我们两个人吃不了。
examples.en: There's too much food; the two of us can't finish it.
examples.analysis: 吃不了 = verb + 不 + 了 (liǎo): 'can't eat it all', because there is more than we can manage. This 了 is read liǎo and follows 不. It is a different word from the 了 (le) in 太多了 earlier in the sentence, which belongs to the 太…了 pattern ('too much').

examples.en: I've got something on tomorrow, so I can't make it.
examples.analysis: 来不了 = 'can't come'. Here something outside your control stops you (you are busy), not a lack of skill. Swap 不 for 得 to get 'can': 来得了. A short, natural way to decline an invitation without a long explanation.

examples.zh: 这么多东西，你一个人拿得了吗？
examples.en: That's a lot of stuff. Can you carry it all by yourself?
examples.analysis: 拿得了吗 asks 'can you manage to carry it?': verb + 得 + 了 (liǎo) is the positive form, and it often appears in questions like this one. The negative answer would be 拿不了. 吗 turns the whole thing into a yes/no question.

collocations.en: can't finish eating; can't eat it

related.en: particle for a finished action or a change (吃了 'ate'); a different word, read le
to finish: 吃不完 = can't finish the amount; 吃不了 also covers other reasons you can't eat something (我吃不了辣 'I can't eat spicy food')

meaning: (preposition) 把 + thing + verb: do something to a specific thing

senses.en: 把 + object + verb + result: handle, move or change a specific thing (把药吃了)
very common in requests and warnings: 请把…, 别把… (请把门关上)

examples.en: I've already taken the medicine.
examples.analysis: 把 moves the object 药 in front of the verb: 把 + 药 + 吃 + 了. The object is a specific thing both people know about (the medicine). The verb is not left bare; 了 follows it, and a result or a place usually does the same job. Adverbs such as 已经 normally go before 把, not before the verb.

examples.en: Where did you put your phone?
examples.analysis: 把 + 手机 + 放在 + place: this pattern is the usual way to say where something was put. The question word 哪儿 stays in the place slot, where the answer would go. 了 marks the putting as done.

examples.en: Don't put things here.
examples.analysis: 别 and other negatives normally go before 把, not before the verb: 别把…, 没把…, 不把…. 东西 is the object and 放在这儿 'put at this spot' ends the sentence, so the verb has a place after it.

related.en: passive: the affected thing becomes the subject (手机被偷了); 把 keeps the doer as the subject

meaning: straight, not crooked; main; proper (adjective)

senses.en: straight; not tilted or crooked; squarely placed (挂得很正, 放正)
main; principal, only in set words (正门 main entrance, 正餐 main meal)
proper; correct; normal (in words like 正确 correct, 正常 normal)

examples.en: This picture isn't hanging quite straight.
examples.analysis: 挂得不太正: verb + 得 + a description of how it hangs. 正 is an adjective of position here: not tilted, lined up properly. 不太 'not very' softens it, so the picture is slightly crooked rather than badly wrong.

examples.en: Please set the chair straight.
examples.analysis: 放正 = 放 'to put' + 正 as the result: the chair ends up squarely in place. It is the adjective after a verb, and the request uses 把 to bring 椅子 in front of the verb. 请 makes it polite.

examples.en: Take a look. Is it straight now?
examples.analysis: 正不正 is the A-not-A question: adjective + 不 + adjective, 'straight or not?'. It checks the result of an adjustment, like after moving a picture. 看看 is the relaxed 'have a look'.

related.en: straight as a line (a straight road, a straight back); 正 is about not being tilted or off-centre
in the middle of doing; a different entry, where 正 is an adverb
normal; as it should be

meaning: measure word for animals (cat, bird, dog) and one of a pair (shoe, eye, hand)

senses.en: for animals, especially small ones: 一只猫, 一只鸟, 两只狗
one of a pair: 一只鞋 one shoe, 一只手 one hand, 一只眼睛 one eye

examples.en: I've got a cat.
examples.analysis: 一只猫 = number + 只 + noun. 只 is the measure word for a cat, and for most pets and birds; it is needed between a number and the noun, just as 个 is in 一个人. 养 'to keep (a pet)' + 了 reads as 'I have got a cat'.

examples.zh: 我有一只眼睛看不太清楚。
examples.en: One of my eyes can't see very clearly.
examples.analysis: Here 只 counts one of a pair: 我有一只眼睛… = 'I have one eye that…', i.e. one of my two eyes. The second half, 看不太清楚 'can't see very clearly', describes that eye. This is what a patient might say to a doctor. For both eyes you could say 两只眼睛.

examples.en: How old is this dog?
examples.analysis: 这 + 只 + 狗: the measure word sits between the demonstrative and the noun, as it does after a number. A dog can take 只 or 条. 几岁 is the natural way to ask the age of a young child or a pet; 了 shows the age now.

related.en: the all-purpose measure word, used when you don't know a specific one
for long, thin things and fish (一条鱼); dogs take 条 or 只
a pair: 一双鞋 'a pair of shoes'; 只 counts one of them

meaning: (passive) by: thing + 被 + (doer) + verb (我的杯子被打破了)

senses.en: A + 被 + (doer) + verb: A has something done to it (杯子被打破了)
the doer can be named (被小王借走了) or left out (被打破了)

examples.en: My cup got broken.
examples.analysis: 杯子 is what the action happened to, so it comes first as the subject; 被 + 打破 makes the passive. No doer is named, which is fine with 被 when the doer is unknown or does not matter. 被 often, though not always, reports something unwelcome, as here.

examples.en: This book has been borrowed by Xiao Wang.
examples.analysis: With a named doer the order is A + 被 + doer + verb: 书 被 小王 借走. 借走 'borrow and take away' carries a result (走), so the sentence is complete. In plain terms: Xiao Wang has the book now.

examples.en: I was moved by what he said.
examples.analysis: A passive with a good feeling: 被 + 他的话 (what moved me) + 感动 'be moved'. 被 is not only for bad events. What causes the feeling goes right after 被, and 了 shows the feeling has happened. The active version is 他的话感动了我.

related.en: the active partner: 他打破了我的杯子 / 他把我的杯子打破了
spoken passive; the doer must be named (叫孩子打破了)
also a spoken passive (让雨淋了); the doer must be named

meaning: to be; to become (成为, 分为); 'is' in notices and formal writing

senses.en: to be (formal, in notices and written style): 时间为…, 价格为…
to become; to be divided into (成为, 分为)

examples.zh: 会议时间为明天下午三点。
examples.en: The meeting time is 3 p.m. tomorrow.
examples.analysis: In notices and formal emails 为 stands in for 是: 会议时间为… = 'the meeting time is…'. Read it wéi. In ordinary talk you would say 会议时间是… or 会议明天下午三点开始. After this 为 you typically find a time, a number, an amount or a name.

examples.en: This book is divided into three parts.
examples.analysis: 分为 = 'divide into': 分 is the action and 为 marks what it becomes, here 三个部分. This pattern is common in books, reports and explanations. Read 为 as wéi, not wèi.

examples.en: She wants to become a doctor.
examples.analysis: 成为 'become' is one word: 成 'turn into' + 为 'be (as)'. What follows is the new role or state, here 医生. 想 + verb phrase says 'wants to'. Read 为 as wéi.

related.en: to be: the everyday word; 为 takes its place only in some formal, written patterns
for; for the sake of (为你好); a different word, read wèi

meaning: (not) at all, before 不/没; and also (formal)

senses.en: not at all: 并不 / 并没有, pushing back on an assumption (我并不累)
and also (formal): joins a second action by the same subject (检查…并开药)

examples.en: I'm not tired at all.
examples.analysis: 并 comes right before the negative 不: 并不累 = 'not tired at all'. It pushes back on what someone has said or assumed (for example, 'you look tired'). When nothing needs correcting, speakers just say 我不累.

examples.en: He never actually said that.
examples.analysis: 并没有 + verb does for the past what 并不 does for the present: a firm denial, against what people think or assume. 没有 negates the event, 过 marks the experience of ever saying it, and 句 counts sentences.

examples.zh: 医生检查了他的眼睛，并给他开了药。
examples.en: The doctor examined his eyes and prescribed him some medicine.
examples.analysis: Here 并 is 'and also', linking two actions by the same subject, 检查 then 开药. It is a written, report-style link. In casual speech people just run the clauses together with a comma, or add 然后.

related.en: and moreover: a separate word; 并 mostly links verb phrases with the same subject, while 并且 also links adjectives and clauses (他聪明并且努力)
actually: states the real situation, but without the 'not at all' push of 并不

meaning: to need; to require; needs (what is needed)

senses.en: to need (需要 + noun or verb: 需要帮忙, 需要休息)
needs; what is needed (大家的需要)

examples.en: Do you need help?
examples.analysis: 需要 + 帮忙 = 'need help'; 吗 makes it a yes/no question. It is a polite, neutral way to check whether someone needs help. 帮忙 is a verb-object word, 'to help out', and it works fine after 需要.

examples.zh: 你不需要马上决定，可以再想想。
examples.en: You don't need to decide right away; you can think it over.
examples.analysis: 不需要 + verb = 'don't need to…': it says the thing is not necessary, which is gentler than a ban. 马上 'right away' goes before 决定. The second half gives the alternative: 再想想 'think it over some more'.

examples.zh: 我们先听听大家的需要吧。
examples.en: Let's first hear what everyone needs.
examples.analysis: Here 需要 is a noun, 'needs', after 的: 大家的需要 = 'everyone's needs'. 听听 is the relaxed 'have a listen'; 先 'first' and 吧 make it a friendly suggestion.

related.en: to want; to need, more casual (我要休息)
must; has no alternative, stronger than 需要

meaning: to die; extremely (after an adjective: 饿死了); rigid

senses.en: to die; to be dead (花死了, 鱼会死)
extremely, after a feeling or state: 饿死了 starving, 累死了 exhausted (colloquial)
rigid; fixed (in words like 死板 rigid, 死机 a computer freezing up)

examples.en: All the flowers I was growing have died.
examples.analysis: 死 is the plain verb 'to die', here for plants. 都 'all' goes before it and 了 marks the change from alive to dead. 我养的花 is a verb phrase + 的 that says which flowers. For a person, 死 is blunt; 去世 is the gentler word.

examples.zh: 我饿死了，我们先吃饭吧。
examples.en: I'm starving! Let's eat first.
examples.analysis: 饿死了 is a colloquial 'extremely hungry'. 死 after an adjective turns up the degree and is not literal, and 了 follows it. It is common with unpleasant states such as 累, 热 and 饿. 先…吧 suggests doing it first.

examples.en: Fish die once they leave the water.
examples.analysis: 离开水就会死: 离开水 'leaving the water' is the condition, 就 links it to the result, and 会 says it will happen. This is a general fact, so there is no 了; 死 here is the literal verb.

related.en: to pass away: the gentle word for people
to live; alive

meaning: (spoken passive) by: thing + 叫 + doer + verb (杯子叫孩子打破了)

senses.en: spoken passive: A + 叫 + doer + verb, 'A was … by the doer' (手机叫弟弟拿走了)
the doer must be named, even if only as 人 'someone' (钱包叫人拿走了)

examples.en: Someone has taken my wallet.
examples.analysis: 叫 works like 被 here, but the doer slot cannot be empty: 叫 + 人 + 拿走, with 人 'someone' in it. With 被 you could say 钱包被拿走了 and name nobody. 叫 gives a spoken, informal tone.

examples.en: Who has driven your car off?
examples.analysis: Because 叫 needs a doer, a question can fill that slot with 谁 'who': 叫谁开走了. 开走 'drive away' carries a result, so the verb is complete. The thing affected, 你的车, comes first as the topic.

examples.zh: 那个杯子叫孩子打破了。
examples.en: That cup got broken by the child.
examples.analysis: 叫 + 孩子 + 打破: the doer 孩子 is named, then a verb with a result (打破 'broke'). The cup comes first as the topic. In writing and formal speech 被 is the usual choice; 叫 belongs to casual talk.

related.en: the neutral/written passive; the doer is optional
also a spoken passive (and 'to let'); the doer must be named

meaning: to begin; to start; a beginning

senses.en: to begin; to start (开始 + verb, or on its own: 电影开始了)
a beginning; a start (一个开始)

examples.en: What time does the movie start?
examples.analysis: 开始 stands on its own as a verb: 'the movie starts', with nothing after it. The time word 几点 goes before the verb. Use 几点开始 for films, meetings and classes.

examples.en: I started learning Chinese last year.
examples.analysis: 从 + time + 开始 + verb: 'from that time on, began to do'. 从去年 gives the starting point and 开始 leads into what began, 学中文. 开始 + verb is the usual way to say 'start doing something'.

examples.zh: 这只是一个开始，后面还有很多工作。
examples.en: This is only the beginning; there's still a lot of work ahead.
examples.analysis: Here 开始 is a noun, 'a beginning', counted by 个: 一个开始. 只是 'only' keeps the claim modest, and 后面 'what comes next' leads into the second half, which says there is more work to do.

related.en: to end; to finish
the opening part of something (of a story, a letter)

meaning: just that, the only thing is (+ small drawback); even if; is exactly

senses.en: but; the only thing is… (adds a small drawback after something good)
even if (就是…也…)
is exactly; is precisely (X 就是 Y)

examples.zh: 这个房子很好，就是有点儿贵。
examples.en: This place is really nice; it's just a bit expensive.
examples.analysis: After a positive statement, 就是 brings in the one small drawback: 'the only thing is…'. What follows is mild (有点儿贵), which signals a minor problem. 就是 is more casual than 但是.

examples.en: Even if you don't say it, I know.
examples.analysis: 就是… 也… = 'even if…, still…'. 就是 opens a condition that the speaker is ready to accept, and 也 in the second half says the result stays the same. This is a spoken, emphatic pattern.

examples.en: This is exactly the book I'm looking for.
examples.analysis: X 就是 Y stresses identity: 'is none other than'. The phrase 我要找的 'what I'm looking for' is the topic, and 就是 makes the match emphatic, like pointing and saying 'that's the one'.

related.en: it's just that…: a little more neutral than 就是 for the 'small drawback' use
but; however (mild)
even if; the more formal version of the 'even if' use

meaning: to hope; a hope

senses.en: to hope (希望 + clause: 希望明天不下雨)
hope; chance of success (有希望, 没有希望)

examples.en: We all hope you can come.
examples.analysis: 希望 + a full clause: what is hoped has its own subject (你) and verb. No linking word is needed before the clause. 都 'all' goes before 希望, and 能 inside the clause means 'be able to'.

examples.en: I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.
examples.analysis: With no subject, 希望 + clause is a casual wish: the 'I' is understood. The weather clause 明天不下雨 needs no subject of its own. To say you hope something won't happen, put the negative inside the clause, as here.

examples.en: Don't worry, we still have hope.
examples.analysis: Here 希望 is a noun, 'hope', the object of 有: 有希望 = 'there's hope, it's promising'. 还 'still' keeps it alive after a setback, and 别急 'no need to rush or panic' comes first as the reassurance.

related.en: disappointed; to lose hope
to want to: about your own wish to act; 希望 is about what you hope will happen

meaning: of course; naturally; only natural

senses.en: of course; naturally (当然可以, 我当然要去)
only natural; to be expected (是当然的)

examples.en: Of course; please have a seat.
examples.analysis: As a reply, 当然可以 = 'of course you may'. 当然 stands before the word it confirms (可以). The second half, 您请坐, is the polite invitation; 您 is the respectful 'you'.

examples.zh: 这么好的机会，我当然要去。
examples.en: A chance this good: of course I'm going.
examples.analysis: 当然 sits before 要去 in the normal adverb position, after the subject 我. It says the decision is obvious, given the reason in the first half. 要 here means 'want to, intend to'.

examples.en: It's only natural that he's unhappy.
examples.analysis: As an adjective, 当然 means 'natural, to be expected'. Pattern: statement + 是当然的 = 'it's natural that…'. 他不高兴 is the statement and 是当然的 is the comment on it.

related.en: definitely; for sure: about certainty, not about the answer being obvious
natural; naturally, without effort

meaning: line, row (of text); line of work. Read háng, not xíng

senses.en: for lines of text and rows: 第一行 the first line, 三十行 thirty lines
line of work; trade (这一行, 哪一行, 干这行): spoken, after 这, 哪 or a similar word
firm; business (in 银行 bank)

examples.zh: 请在第一行写你的名字。
examples.en: Please write your name on the first line.
examples.analysis: 行 is read háng here: a measure word for lines of text, so 第一行 = 'the first line'. 在 + 第一行 + 写 gives the place before the verb, 'write on the first line'. 请 makes it polite, as on a form.

examples.en: There are thirty lines on this page.
examples.analysis: 三十行 = number + measure word 行, 'thirty lines'. 一共 'altogether' sums it up. 行 counts rows of text, or rows in a table; here the page 这一页 comes first as the topic.

examples.zh: 我做这一行已经十年了。
examples.en: I've been in this line of work for ten years.
examples.analysis: Here 行 means 'line of work, trade': 这一行 'this field'. 做这一行 = 'to work in this line'. 已经…了 shows the ten years have built up to now. Ask 你是做哪一行的？ for 'what line of work are you in?'.

related.en: a row of seats or people (第一排 'front row'); 行 is for lines of text and table rows
OK; all right (行不行？); a different word, read xíng

meaning: when; at the time of (after a clause); o'clock (formal); time

senses.en: when; while; at the time (clause + 时): 开车时, 不舒服时
o'clock, in formal writing: 三时 = 三点
time; period (in words like 有时, 当时, 同时, 小时)

examples.en: Don't look at your phone while driving.
examples.analysis: A verb phrase + 时 = 'when / while…': 开车时 'when driving'. The time clause comes first, the main clause after it. 时 is a shorter, more formal version of 的时候, common in signs, rules and advice. 不要 is a direct 'don't'.

examples.zh: 不舒服时，请马上告诉医生。
examples.en: If you feel unwell, please tell the doctor right away.
examples.analysis: The same pattern with an adjective: 不舒服时 = 'when (you) feel unwell', which reads as 'if' too. 请 + 马上 + verb is a polite instruction, the kind a clinic notice or a doctor gives.

examples.en: The meeting starts at 3 p.m.
examples.analysis: In formal writing 时 can stand for 点, the clock hour: 三时 = 三点 'three o'clock'. You see it in notices, schedules and the news; in speech people say 三点. The time phrase comes before the verb 开始.

related.en: time, moment: the spoken way is …的时候
o'clock in speech (三点); 时 is the formal written form
time (the amount, or a point in time)

meaning: to happen; to occur; to take place

senses.en: to happen; to occur (发生 + event): 发生事故, 发生什么事了
to arise, in written style: 发生变化 a change takes place

examples.en: What happened yesterday?
examples.analysis: 发生 + 什么事 = 'what happened'. The new event comes after the verb, as its object, and 了 marks it as having happened. A time word such as 昨天 goes first. Without 昨天, 发生什么事了？ is what you ask someone who looks upset.

examples.zh: 这样的事不会再发生了。
examples.en: This kind of thing won't happen again.
examples.analysis: Here the event 这样的事 is already known, so it comes before the verb as the subject. 不会再…了 = 'won't … any more': 会 predicts, 再 'again', and the final 了 says that situation is over. A typical reassurance after an apology.

examples.en: There's been an accident up ahead.
examples.analysis: Place word first, then 发生了 + the event: 事故 'accident' (traffic or workplace). A new event is normally introduced after the verb, as its object. A driver or a passenger might say this when the road ahead is blocked.

related.en: to appear; to emerge (出现问题 'a problem appears')
(spoken) something bad has happened; to have an accident

meaning: everything; all (usually followed by 都)

senses.en: everything; all things (一切都好, 一切都准备好了)
all; every, before a noun (written style): 一切问题, 一切费用

examples.en: Everything will be fine.
examples.analysis: 一切 is the subject, 'everything', and it is usually followed by 都 'all', which sits before the verb. 会…的 predicts the future and reassures: 会好的 = 'it will turn out OK'.

examples.zh: 你放心，一切都准备好了。
examples.en: Don't worry; everything is ready.
examples.analysis: 一切 'everything' is the subject, followed by 都. 准备好了 = 'prepared and done' (好 shows the result). 你放心 is a set comforting phrase, literally 'you put your heart at ease'.

examples.zh: 你对这里的一切都满意吗？
examples.en: Are you satisfied with everything here?
examples.analysis: Here 一切 is modified: 这里的一切 = 'everything here', after 对 'about / with'. 都满意吗 asks about the whole lot. This is the sort of question a hotel or a service gives its guests.

related.en: all; every: goes before a noun (所有的人)
the whole; all of it
all; the word that usually follows 一切

meaning: just; merely; but, it's just that

senses.en: only; merely; just (只是 + verb or noun)
but; it's just that… (adds a small reservation)

examples.en: I'm only asking; don't be angry.
examples.analysis: 只是 before a verb = 'just, merely': it plays down the action. 问问 is the relaxed, short 'ask'. The second half, 你别生气, says what the speaker is worried about, and 只是 explains that nothing more is meant.

examples.zh: 这个办法不错，只是有点儿麻烦。
examples.en: This is a good approach; it's just a bit of a hassle.
examples.analysis: After a positive remark, 只是 adds a small reservation: 'but, it's just that…'. The thing that follows is minor. It does the same job as 就是, just a little more neutral.

examples.zh: 他不是不想来，只是没有时间。
examples.en: It's not that he doesn't want to come; he just has no time.
examples.analysis: 不是…，只是… = 'it's not that…, it's just that…'. The first half rejects a possible assumption (he doesn't want to come), and 只是 gives the real reason. 没有时间 'has no time' is the actual cause.

related.en: for the 'it's just that…' use, a bit more casual
but; however (mild)
only (adverb before a verb: 我只有一个); a different entry

meaning: measure word for schools, hospitals; 所 + verb + 的 'what…'; place (诊所)

senses.en: for schools, hospitals and other institutions (一所学校), also houses
所 + verb + 的 = 'what / that which …' (我所知道的); careful or written style
place; office (bound, in 诊所 clinic, 厕所 toilet)

examples.en: This university is very famous.
examples.analysis: 所 is the specific measure word for schools and universities: 这 + 所 + 大学, the same slot as 个. In casual speech 个 also works, but 一所学校 is the standard phrase. Use 个 for everyday objects.

examples.en: He works at a hospital.
examples.analysis: 一所医院 = 'a hospital'. 所 counts institutions here. 在 + place + 工作 says where he works. For hospitals you will also hear 一家医院 with 家, which is very common too.

examples.zh: 我所知道的，都告诉你了。
examples.en: I've told you everything I know.
examples.analysis: 所 + verb + 的 = 'what (I) know': 所知道的 turns a verb phrase into 'the thing known'. It carries almost the same meaning as 我知道的 but sounds more careful and formal. 都告诉你了 = 'told you all of it'.

related.en: measure word for shops and companies, also hospitals (一家医院)
so; therefore: a different word
all; every
